sections.heading: When Is Ramadan? 2027 Dates and Why They Change Every Year

blocks.text: Updated: August 2026
Ramadan does not have a fixed date on the calendar most international travelers use.

In 2027, Ramadan in Turkey begins on Monday, February 8, while the first day of Ramazan Bayramı, known internationally as Eid al-Fitr, falls on Tuesday, March 9. That places the entire fasting month unusually early in the Gregorian year compared with the Ramadan dates many travelers remember from a decade ago.
The reason is simple but important: Ramadan follows the Hijri, or Islamic lunar calendar, rather than the Gregorian solar calendar.

Because a lunar year is shorter than a solar year, Ramadan moves approximately ten or eleven days earlier each Gregorian year. Over time, it passes through every season. Someone who remembers long summer Ramadan days in Turkey may encounter the same religious month during much shorter winter days several years later.
This movement affects far more than trivia.
It determines how long daily fasting lasts, when iftar occurs, how Ramadan overlaps with travel seasons and where Ramazan Bayramı falls within the international holiday calendar.
The first thing to understand, however, is the distinction between three dates that travelers frequently mix together:
the beginning of Ramadan, the final fasting day and the beginning of Eid al-Fitr.
They are connected, but they are not the same event.

sections.heading: When Does Ramadan Start in 2027?

blocks.text: In Turkey, Ramadan begins on February 8, 2027.
This corresponds to the first day of Ramadan in the Hijri year 1448.
The fasting month continues through the beginning of March, with March 8 serving as the final day immediately before Ramazan Bayramı begins.
The first day of Ramazan Bayramı is March 9, 2027.
For straightforward trip planning, those are the dates most travelers need to remember:
The distinction between March 8 and March 9 matters because Ramadan itself finishes before the Eid celebration begins.

sections.heading: Why Does Ramadan Start on a Different Date Every Year?

blocks.text: The answer lies in the structure of the Islamic calendar.
The Gregorian calendar used internationally for civil purposes follows the solar year and contains approximately 365 days.
The Hijri calendar is lunar.
A Hijri year contains roughly 354 or 355 days, which makes it around ten to eleven days shorter than a Gregorian year.
That difference accumulates annually.
If Ramadan begins around February 19 one year, it may begin around February 8 the following year. Another year later it moves into late January.
This is not a correction or irregularity.
It is exactly how the calendar is designed to work.
Ramadan therefore does not belong permanently to spring, summer, autumn or winter.
Over a cycle of roughly three decades, the month gradually moves through the entire Gregorian year.

sections.heading: The Recent Dates Show the Pattern Clearly

blocks.text: Looking at three consecutive years makes the shift much easier to understand.
This table is more useful than memorizing one year's date because it reveals the underlying pattern.
If you are planning Turkey several years in advance, a rough mental rule is that Ramadan will usually move around ten or eleven days earlier each Gregorian year.
For confirmed travel planning, however, use the officially published calendar for the relevant year rather than calculating dates yourself.

sections.heading: Does Ramadan Begin at Midnight?

blocks.text: This is where the calendar becomes slightly more nuanced.
In Islamic tradition, a religious day begins at sunset rather than at midnight in the conventional Gregorian sense.
This means the spiritual beginning of Ramadan occurs with the evening preceding the first full fasting day.
The practical fasting schedule, however, is usually communicated using the date of the first daytime fast.
So when a Turkey calendar says Ramadan begins on February 8, 2027, travelers generally understand February 8 as the first fasting day.
The preceding evening leads into Ramadan.
This distinction explains why some international references appear to describe Ramadan as beginning “on the evening of” one date while calendars list the following day as Day 1.
They are describing two parts of the same transition.

sections.heading: Why Can Ramadan Dates Differ Between Countries?

blocks.text: Another source of confusion appears when travelers search several websites and discover slightly different dates.
Historically and religiously, the beginning of an Islamic lunar month is associated with the appearance of the new crescent moon, known as the hilal.

Different countries and religious authorities can use different methodologies for determining the beginning of a lunar month. Some emphasize local or regional moon sighting, while others use astronomical calculations or unified calendar systems.
As a result, the first day of Ramadan can occasionally differ by a day between countries or Muslim communities.
That does not mean one travel calendar is necessarily “wrong.”
It may reflect a different accepted method of determining the lunar month's beginning.
For a traveler visiting Turkey, the most practical approach is to follow Turkey's officially used religious calendar when planning local dates.

sections.heading: How Turkey Determines the Ramadan Calendar

blocks.text: Turkey uses a nationally coordinated religious calendar published through the Presidency of Religious Affairs, commonly known as Diyanet.
Its lunar calendar calculations follow an internationally coordinated method that uses astronomical criteria concerning the visibility of the new crescent.
This creates one published Ramadan calendar for practical use across Turkey.
For visitors, that is useful because hotel operations, religious observances and the national Ramazan Bayramı calendar can all be understood from the same date framework.
You do not need to conduct your own moon-sighting research before booking a flight to Istanbul.
Follow the Turkish calendar for a Turkey journey.

sections.heading: Ramadan Is the Ninth Month, Not the Name of the Holiday After It

blocks.text: This terminology causes persistent confusion.
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and the period during which Muslims observe fasting.
When Ramadan concludes, Eid al-Fitr begins.
In Turkey, Eid al-Fitr is normally called Ramazan Bayramı.
You may also hear the traditional expression Şeker Bayramı, although Ramazan Bayramı is the more direct religious-calendar name.
So:
Ramadan = the fasting month
Ramazan Bayramı = the holiday immediately following Ramadan
They should not be described as interchangeable events.
This becomes particularly important for travelers because the practical effect of Ramazan Bayramı can be different from the fasting month itself.

sections.heading: How Long Does Ramadan Last?

blocks.text: A Hijri month contains either 29 or 30 days.
That duration follows the lunar calendar rather than the fixed month lengths familiar from the Gregorian calendar.
For visitors, the important concept is that Ramadan lasts approximately one lunar month, beginning with 1 Ramadan and concluding immediately before 1 Shawwal.
The first day of Shawwal is Eid al-Fitr.
This is why simply adding “30 days” to a Ramadan start date is not always the ideal method for determining future travel dates.
Use the published religious calendar.

sections.heading: What Is Kadir Gecesi and When Is It in 2027?

blocks.text: Kadir Gecesi, known in English as the Night of Power or Laylat al-Qadr, is one of the most important nights within Ramadan.
In Turkey's 2027 religious calendar, Kadir Gecesi falls on March 5.
Its religious significance comes from Islamic belief concerning the revelation of the Quran, and mosques may be especially active on this night.
For this particular article, however, the important point is calendrical rather than a detailed explanation of worship practices.
Kadir Gecesi occurs inside Ramadan, close to its conclusion.
It is not the same as Ramazan Bayramı and does not mark the end of the fasting month.

sections.heading: Why Ramadan Sometimes Feels Much Harder in One Year Than Another

blocks.text: The moving calendar changes the fasting experience because daylight varies enormously by season.
Ramadan falling in midsummer can produce significantly longer periods between the pre-dawn meal and sunset.
When Ramadan falls in February, as it does in Turkey in 2027, daylight is considerably shorter than during a June or July Ramadan.
This is one of the most interesting consequences of using a lunar calendar.
Over a person's lifetime, Ramadan is not always observed under the same seasonal conditions.
A Muslim in Istanbul may experience years with long summer fasts and, decades later, much shorter winter fasts.
The religious month remains Ramadan.
The physical day surrounding it changes.

sections.heading: When Will Ramadan Return to the Same Season?

blocks.text: Because Ramadan moves about ten or eleven days earlier each Gregorian year, it takes roughly 32 to 33 years to move through the full seasonal cycle and return to approximately the same point of the solar calendar.
This means people can experience markedly different versions of Ramadan during their lifetime.
Winter Ramadan.
Autumn Ramadan.
Summer Ramadan.
Spring Ramadan.
For travel publishers, this is also why content describing Ramadan as permanently associated with one climate condition becomes outdated.
The month itself moves.
A good evergreen Ramadan article must explain the calendar mechanism rather than tying the religious period permanently to one season.

sections.heading: Why the Date Matters for Turkey Travel Planning

blocks.text: This page is deliberately not another guide to traveling during Ramadan; that topic has its own owner article.
There is nevertheless one important calendar-level reason visitors need the date.
You need to know whether your travel period overlaps:

ordinary Ramadan days,
the final days of Ramadan,
or Ramazan Bayramı.
Those periods are not operationally identical.
For example, a traveler arriving on March 3, 2027 is visiting during Ramadan.
A traveler arriving on March 10 is visiting during the Ramazan Bayramı holiday.
Those descriptions should not be used interchangeably when researching transportation or local schedules.

Travelers combining the dates with a broader cultural journey can consider Turkey private cultural itineraries, while keeping the more detailed behavioral guidance on the dedicated Ramadan travel page.

sections.heading: Does Ramadan Always Begin About Eleven Days Earlier?

blocks.text: “About” is the important word.
The Hijri year is generally ten or eleven days shorter than the Gregorian year, so Ramadan shifts accordingly.
That does not mean you should calculate distant Ramadan dates simply by subtracting eleven days repeatedly.
Gregorian leap years, whether individual Hijri months have 29 or 30 days and the calendar methodology being used can influence the exact civil date.
For rough understanding, the ten-to-eleven-day rule works extremely well.
For tickets, hotels or religious planning, use the confirmed calendar for that year.

sections.heading: Ramadan Can Occur Twice in One Gregorian Year

blocks.text: This sounds impossible until you remember that the Islamic year is shorter.

Because the Hijri calendar continuously moves backward through the Gregorian calendar, there are rare occasions when one Ramadan begins very early in January and the next Ramadan begins again near the end of December in the same Gregorian year.
The same principle can produce Gregorian years containing two instances of other Islamic calendar events.
This is not an extra Ramadan being added.
It is simply the mathematical consequence of fitting shorter lunar years inside a longer solar calendar.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Ramadan Dates

blocks.text: Ramadan begins in Turkey on Monday, February 8, 2027. This is the first fasting day according to Turkey's official religious calendar. The month continues into March, immediately followed by the three-day Ramazan Bayramı celebration.

sections.heading: 2. When does Ramadan end in Turkey in 2027?

blocks.text: The Ramadan period reaches its conclusion immediately before Ramazan Bayramı begins. In the 2027 Turkish calendar, March 8 is the day preceding the holiday, while March 9 marks the first day of Ramazan Bayramı.

sections.heading: 3. When is Eid al-Fitr in Turkey in 2027?

blocks.text: Eid al-Fitr, called Ramazan Bayramı in Turkey, begins on Tuesday, March 9, 2027. The three official holiday days fall on March 9, March 10 and March 11, following the completion of the Ramadan fasting month.

sections.heading: 4. Why does Ramadan change date every year?

blocks.text: Ramadan follows the Islamic Hijri lunar calendar, whose year is roughly ten or eleven days shorter than the Gregorian solar year. As a result, Ramadan moves earlier through the Gregorian calendar annually and eventually passes through every season.

sections.heading: 5. Is Ramadan always 30 days long?

blocks.text: No. Islamic lunar months can contain either 29 or 30 days. Travelers should therefore use the officially published religious calendar rather than assuming every Ramadan ends exactly thirty Gregorian days after the listed first fasting day.

sections.heading: 6. Why do some countries start Ramadan on different days?

blocks.text: Different religious authorities can use different methods involving crescent visibility, local moon sighting or astronomical calculations. As a result, Ramadan may occasionally begin one day apart in different countries or communities even though everyone is observing the same Islamic month.

sections.heading: 7. When is Kadir Gecesi in Turkey in 2027?

blocks.text: Turkey's official 2027 religious calendar places Kadir Gecesi on March 5. Known internationally as Laylat al-Qadr or the Night of Power, it occurs toward the end of Ramadan but does not itself mark the end of the fasting month.

sections.heading: 8. Does Ramadan begin at sunset or in the morning?

blocks.text: An Islamic calendar day begins at sunset, so Ramadan enters religiously on the evening preceding the first full fasting day. Travel calendars normally identify the following civil date as the first day of Ramadan because that is when the first daytime fast occurs.

sections.heading: 9. When will Ramadan begin in 2028?

blocks.text: In Turkey's published religious calendar, Ramadan begins on January 28, 2028. This illustrates the normal lunar-calendar movement, placing the beginning approximately eleven days earlier than its February 8 position in 2027.

sections.heading: 10. Does Ramadan happen in the same season every year?

blocks.text: No. Because the Islamic year is shorter than the Gregorian year, Ramadan gradually travels through winter, autumn, summer and spring. It takes roughly three decades for the month to cycle back to approximately the same seasonal position.

sections.heading: 11. Is Ramadan the same as Ramazan Bayrami?

blocks.text: No. Ramadan is the Islamic fasting month, while Ramazan Bayramı is Turkey's name for Eid al-Fitr, the celebration beginning immediately after Ramadan ends. Travelers should keep the two periods separate when checking dates and holiday schedules.

sections.heading: 12. Which Ramadan dates should tourists remember for Turkey in 2027?

blocks.text: The two most useful dates are February 8, when Ramadan begins, and March 9, when Ramazan Bayramı begins. Travelers with dates near early March should also check whether their stay overlaps the final Ramadan days or the holiday period.

The two most useful dates are February 8, when Ramadan begins, and March 9, when Ramazan Bayramı begins. Travelers with dates near early March should also check whether their stay overlaps the final Ramadan days or the holiday period.
